q-350845.name: Question 2
q-350845.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the following result:

$$
\int {e}^{px+q}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{p}{e}^{px+q}+C
$$

We proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to \infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-3x+2}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{-3x+2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{[-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-3x+2}]}_{0}^{a} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-3a+2}+\frac{1}{3}{e}^{2}) \\  & =(\frac{{e}^{2}}{3}-\frac{{e}^{2}}{3}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-3a})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall the end behavior of the function $y={e}^{-3x}$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }{e}^{-3x}=\infty $

- ${lim}_{x\to \infty }{e}^{-3x}=0$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14260591/assets/425e55256d2e53db1fce6684e2b7b05e8b487d5107dd4abacb8cf17add287c23.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-3x+2}\,\text{d}x & =(\frac{{e}^{2}}{3}-\frac{{e}^{2}}{3}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-3a}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2}}{3}-\frac{{e}^{2}}{3}\cdot 0 \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-6296.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the following result:

$$
\int {e}^{px+q}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{p}{e}^{px+q}+C
$$

We proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to \infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }{e}^{-x}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{a}{e}^{-x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{[-{e}^{-x}]}_{1}^{a} \\  & =-{lim}_{a\to \infty }{[{e}^{-x}]}_{1}^{a} \\  & =-({lim}_{a\to \infty }\frac{1}{{e}^{a}}-{e}^{-1})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall the end behavior of the function $y=\frac{1}{{e}^{x}},$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{1}{{e}^{x}}=\infty $

- ${lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{1}{{e}^{x}}=0$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14260591/assets/a7d8d7829a2f4160f3e4e6935efd6294ed696eba0d9003c9b7cba379bae21ba9.png)

$$

$$

q-152231.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the following result:

$$
\int {b}^{\,px+q}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{p\operatorname{ln}⁡(b)}{b}^{\,px+q}+C
$$

We proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to -\infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}{5}^{x/2}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}{5}^{x/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[\frac{2\cdot {5}^{x/2}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}]}_{a}^{0} \\  & =\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[{5}^{x/2}]}_{a}^{0} \\  & =\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }(1-{5}^{a/2}) \\  & =\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}\cdot (1-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{5}^{a/2})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall the end behavior of the function $y={5}^{x/2}$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }{5}^{x/2}=0$

- ${lim}_{x\to \infty }{5}^{x/2}=\infty $

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14260591/assets/141d1745dc939ca63155ca3313257f385af6d3c505c16bd63ba3b91e1e0ba64b.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$

q-152255.worked_solution:
First, we substitute $u=\sqrt{x}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}\,⟹\,2\text{d}u=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\text{d}x.
$$

Since $u\to \infty $ when $x\to \infty ,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=\sqrt{x}$ is as follows:

| $x$ | $0$ | $\infty $ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\infty $ |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{{3}^{-\sqrt{x}}}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x & =2{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{3}^{-u}\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to \infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{{3}^{-\sqrt{x}}}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x & =2{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{3}^{-u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{3}^{-u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[-\frac{{3}^{-u}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}]}_{0}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[{3}^{-u}]}_{0}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\cdot ({lim}_{a\to \infty }\frac{1}{{3}^{a}}-1)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, recall the end behavior of the function $y=\frac{1}{{3}^{x}},$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{1}{{3}^{x}}=\infty $

- ${lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{1}{{3}^{x}}=0$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14260591/assets/ff41c6fa5858f45e76a4d4fec0f0a8080300b69fcb632df60141d93c66f3cdd9.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{{3}^{-\sqrt{x}}}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x & =-\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\cdot ({lim}_{a\to \infty }\frac{1}{{3}^{a}}-1) \\  & =-\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\cdot (0-1) \\  & =\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}.\end{aligned}
$$
